title: Talking like a Brazilian
goal: Round off the module with the layer grammar books don't teach: the little words, exclamations and speech habits that make your Portuguese sound alive, not translated.
bekal: using fifteen typically Brazilian fillers and exclamations
softening requests and refusals in a natural way
recognizing the small-talk phrases you'll hear every day

notes: **Cara is the most common way for friends to address each other in Brazil.** It literally means "face", but it's used like "man", "dude" or "mate" — and these days for men and women alike. In São Paulo people also say *mano*; in Rio Grande do Sul, *tchê*. ⚠️ Don't use it in formal settings.

**Valeu** is the casual "thanks". Literally "it was worth it", and between friends it's heard far more than *obrigado* — which sounds a little more formal. Good replies: *Que isso*, *Imagina*, or *Valeu você*.
**Mandou bem** literally "you sent well", means "you did great, nice work". One of the most common compliments among young Brazilians. Its opposite: *mandou mal*.

**Viu? at the end of a sentence isn't a question.** Literally "did you see?", its job is to soften the sentence — roughly like "okay?" or "you know" tacked on in English: "take care, okay?". It's in the same family as *né?* and *tá?*

**Errar faz parte** = "mistakes are part of the process". It's a fitting line to close the module on, because it's the most useful attitude for anyone learning a language — and it happens to be very Brazilian too.

grammars.title: Fillers and exclamations
body: These words have no tidy dictionary meaning, but without them your Portuguese will sound like an airport announcement.
after: **Tipo works exactly like English "like"** — a pause filler while your brain hunts for a word. Using it now and then makes you sound natural; using it in every sentence makes you sound like a teenager.
**Sei lá is the most useful answer when you really don't know.** It's warmer than *não sei*, and often comes with a shrug.

grammars.title: Softening and saying no
body: Brazilians rarely say no directly. These six formulas cover almost every polite refusal.
after: ⚠️ **Depois a gente combina often means "no".** It's a social habit worth understanding: promising a meeting that won't happen is considered more polite than refusing outright — much like an English "we should grab coffee sometime".
And the flip side: when a Brazilian really wants to meet, they'll name **a day and a time** — *Que tal quinta às sete?* That's the sign of a real invitation.

sections.title: Small talk you'll hear every day

head: Português

rows: Have a good day at work!

blocks.text: **Beleza literally means "beauty"**, and it works as a greeting, a reply and a sign of agreement all at once. A complete, perfectly valid Brazilian conversation: *— E aí, beleza? — Beleza! E você? — Beleza.*
*Falou!* is used to end a conversation, not to report that someone spoke. It's like "okay, later" — and often comes together with *valeu*, *abraço* or *até*.
Not cheap slang that goes stale fast — these ten words have lasted for decades and are used across all ages.

blocks.text: **Jeitinho brasileiro** deserves its own explanation. It means the knack of finding a creative way out when the rules get in the way — sometimes warm and clever, sometimes a little bit crooked. Brazilians talk about it with a mix of pride and embarrassment.
*Gostoso* applies to food, weather, naps, even conversations: *uma conversa gostosa* = a lovely chat. ⚠️ Said about **a person**, it means "sexy" — so choose your target carefully.

items: I have a sore throat → *Estou com dor de garganta*
Do I need a prescription? → *Preciso de receita?*
Drink plenty of water → *Bebe bastante água*

blocks.text: Twenty units are behind you. You started with *oi* and now you can tell the story of your childhood, order food, push back on an opinion and turn down an invitation politely. That's no small achievement.

What matters most now isn't more grammar but **more speaking hours**. Brazilian Portuguese has one big advantage at this stage: its speakers are among the most generous in the world toward foreigners who give it a try. You won't be coldly corrected; you'll be cheered on.

blocks.title: Three next steps
items: **Listen every day, even when you don't understand.** Brazilian podcasts, songs and telenovelas. Your ear still needs to get used to real-life speed — and that can't be sped up by reading.

**Find one person to talk to regularly.** One hour of conversation a week is worth more than ten hours of memorizing. If you don't have anyone yet, language-exchange apps are full of Brazilians who want to practice English.

**Move on to A2 with these three things:** the *subjuntivo* (which this module deliberately left alone), two-verb constructions, and vocabulary for your own job or interests. You already have all the basic grammar.

blocks.text: *Errar faz parte.* Mistakes are part of the process. Speak first, polish later.

items: ____ eu cheguei e ele já tinha saído. (and then)
